items.question: How do you assess AlphaEvolve's significance as a milestone in AI's ability to make novel scientific discoveries?
items.object: AlphaEvolve as a milestone in AI scientific discovery
items.answer: Yeah, so it's certainly a key sort of milestone. What we have shown is that an AI model, a large language model, when coupled with a harness, is able to discover new algorithms and not only that, it's basically able to prove new mathematical results which have been studied for many, many years.
quotes: Yeah, so it's certainly a key sort of milestone. What we have shown is that an AI model, a large language model, when coupled with a harness, is able to discover new algorithms and not only that, it's basically able to prove new mathematical results which have been studied for many, many years.

items.question: How do you see the role of the harness around a large language model in enabling scientific discovery through FunSearch?
items.object: The evaluator and search harness around an LLM in FunSearch
items.answer: Around two years back, we had an agent called FunSearch in which we took an LLM and coupled it with an evaluator. The evaluator allowed the LLM to figure out, when it was making new conjectures or coming up with new ideas to solve problems, whether they were hallucinations or brilliant insights. So essentially, in this particular case, hallucinations were great because some of those hallucinations were in fact brilliant new insights that nobody had thought about. This is where the harness comes in: you have this evaluation function and essentially a search protocol associated with the LLM that together are able to come up with completely new discoveries that are really impactful.

The response observes that apparent LLM hallucinations can be a source of genuinely novel scientific insights.

items.question: How do you see AlphaEvolve advancing beyond FunSearch in discovering new algorithms?
items.object: FunSearch and AlphaEvolve
items.answer: FunSearch was our first instantiation of taking a large language model and trying to see if it can discover new algorithms. The models at that time were weaker, right? And the type of search that we were trying to do—we had not explored things much further. So what we asked the LLM to do was essentially try to complete a small function and see if it can do that much better. And surprisingly it was able to discover completely new algorithms that mathematicians had been trying to study for a long time. But the limitation was that the mathematician or researcher had to give a template in which the algorithm should be found. With AlphaEvolve we have removed that restriction. AlphaEvolve is not just searching for a few lines. It's basically looking at whole algorithms themselves, very large pieces of code, and optimizing them over a long period of time. And secondly, FunSearch, our original model, used a lot of function evaluations to make these new discoveries. AlphaEvolve can work with many fewer function calls and, by looking at fewer proposals, it can discover new algorithms much more quickly.

items.question: How do you see improvements in Gemini's understanding of code affecting AlphaEvolve's search for solutions to hard mathematical and computational problems?
items.object: Gemini's improving coding abilities and AlphaEvolve's search effectiveness
items.answer: So, I think, see, we have been evaluating, and as Gemini improves with the various generations, it is becoming much, much better at its understanding of code. Now, if you have a proposal generator which can understand code much more effectively, then it generates proposals which are not only syntactically correct, they are also semantically trying to solve the task. And then you are sampling the different ways in which the task can be solved. So as the baseline model Gemini's abilities to perform coding improve, our sample effectiveness in searching for the right solution on these very hard math and computational problems becomes much better. So if you want to search in a large space, there are two elements. One is the speed of how you can generate these proposals, and then the speed at which you can evaluate those proposals.

items.question: How do you understand the scope of AlphaEvolve’s generality?
items.object: AlphaEvolve’s generality and scope
items.answer: So AlphaEvolve essentially allows you to search not only in terms of the size of what you can search over—you can now discover whole new algorithms—but it also is extremely general in its ability of thinking about algorithms in various different languages. Not only can it search in C++, but it can also do it in Python. It can also do it in Verilog, which is the language for describing chips in chip design. So the generality of AlphaEvolve is in its ability to search these large algorithmic spaces, but also in different syntactic and semantic representations. It is not restricted to a particular language like Python, but it can do that search across many different types of languages and many different types of tasks. The only expectation it has is that you have a function evaluator, that you can quickly evaluate whatever proposal there is and say how good it is.

items.question: What do you find interesting about how the co-scientist system uses Gemini to reproduce the scientific academic process?
items.object: The co-scientist multi-agent system
items.answer: In co-scientist, essentially what you had was Gemini playing the role of the whole scientific academic process: Gemini playing the role of a hypothesis generator, Gemini playing the role of the critique, Gemini playing the role of ranking different ideas, reviewing those ideas, ranking those ideas, and then editing those ideas. So it was Gemini playing all these roles in a multi-agent setup, and these were all Gemini models prompted differently to play different roles. And very interestingly, this combined multi-agent system came up with behavior that went much beyond a single Gemini model's answer. It was able to give much, much better proposals and new ideas compared to a single model.

items.question: How do you explain why co-scientist’s multi-agent system produces better ideas as you give it more computation?
items.object: Co-scientist’s multi-agent approach to refining scientific ideas
items.answer: I think that it is something that is still being studied, but it is a fascinating sort of thing. The one thing that I actually noticed is that, especially with regards to co-scientist, you would run co-scientist on a particular problem and the very first answer that you might get might not be very different from the baseline Gemini model. But what happens is, even as you increase the amount of computation—not just a few minutes or a few hours, but even days—as the whole multi-agent system looks at the solutions and then refines them and tries to rank them, it just becomes much, much better. It might be that there are deep insights or some sort of intuitions that are buried in the tail of the distribution, right? And then somehow Gemini's ability to evaluate which proposal, which idea is better, is much better than its capability to come up with a new idea. It's the same sort of thing in computer science, right? Sometimes we know whether a particular solution is correct or not, but it's very difficult to come up with a solution. So it's the same sort of thing appearing again in this multi-agent setup, that somehow the agents working together are able to extract many more impactful results.

items.question: How do you see the current state of research on AI agent architectures?
items.object: AI agent architectures
items.answer: I think there is going to be more work in agents, right? What we are seeing is basically the very start of research on agents. Whether in AlphaEvolve, you had a generator coupled with an evaluator. The generator was a neural network, a foundational model, an LLM, and the evaluator was even hand-coded, right? But together with an evolutionary search scheme, you were able to get these much more effective results. In co-scientist, you didn't have just one agent; you had multiple agents working in a shared memory. What is the optimal agent configuration? This is still an open research problem.

items.question: Why did you pursue searching for programs with LLMs in FunSearch as an approach to algorithmic discovery?
items.object: FunSearch's use of LLMs to discover interpretable programs
items.answer: So let's go back to the original motivation for why we started working on the first iteration of using LLMs for algorithmic discovery, which was FunSearch. A few years back, as you know, DeepMind has done a lot of work in using AI systems for searching over large spaces. We have done a lot of work in building agents which have been trained using reinforcement learning, which can deal with many complex challenges, from the game of Go to playing StarCraft. We set ourselves a challenge: can we take the same kinds of models, like the AlphaZero family of models, which were extensions of what we had done in Go and the development of AlphaGo? Can we use the same types of models for discovering new algorithms? And we came up with a new agent called AlphaTensor, which was particularly focused on finding solutions for the matrix multiplication problem. We found that this agent was able to improve over the past known results, which had stood for 50 years. But the key question remained: can you do something better, and secondly, can you come up with a solution that is more interpretable? At the same time, when we were looking at practical problems in Google, like how do you schedule jobs in a data center, there has been a lot of work on coming up with new algorithms, and these heuristics have been designed by some of the best researchers and engineers at Google because they have a huge amount of impact in terms of compute utilization. If you use a typical reinforcement learning agent on this kind of problem, you might get better results, but it might come at the cost of interpretability, because now you have a neural network deciding which workloads go to which computers, and if something breaks, then you don't know how to debug this thing. So what engineers would really prefer is that instead of giving them a neural network, you gave them a piece of code that they can interpret and run. And this was essentially the motivation: can we now use LLMs? Instead of searching in the space of specific algorithms, like the matrix multiplication algorithms we had done in AlphaTensor, or coming up with a neural network policy to directly solve the problem, can we come up with an agent which can search in the space of programs and come up with a program that solves this hard problem? The benefit, of course, will be interpretability: you can see the code, you can see what its properties are, and so on. And that's what happened. We found programs that were not only effective, but when the experts actually saw those programs, they could recover insights. For instance, one of the math problems that we had looked at for FunSearch was called the capset problem. This is a problem that Terrence Tao, one of the famous mathematicians, is very interested in, and we collaborated with the mathematician Jordan Ellenberg at NYU. When we looked at the program that FunSearch had produced, he found that there were certain symmetries in the problem that had not been recognized before. Somehow the agent had discovered those and was utilizing those to get a better solution.

items.question: What do you find valuable about mathematics as a way to evaluate AI-generated results?
items.object: Mathematics as a way to evaluate AI-generated results
items.answer: I think math certainly has some properties which are very interesting, right? The fact that it's very precise: you can know whether the property that you are looking for, whether you have found it or not. For matrix multiplication, how many multiplications you require—for a 4x4 matrix, what was known was that you can do it with 49 multiplications; that's Strassen's. And we showed that you can do it by 48. So that's a very precise result, right? There is no arguing about that. It gives you a very crisp way of evaluating how well you have done. And there's no RLHF needed in terms of human feedback, whether this was a nice result or a nice output or not, and you don't need to rely on an LMS score. You just know that you're better.

items.question: Where do you see AlphaEvolve having the greatest potential for real-world impact?
items.object: AlphaEvolve’s suitability for real-world problems
items.answer: I’d say wherever you can find a good function evaluator, wherever you can find an evaluator where you can say, “I really trust this evaluation scheme. If you give me a program, I can tell you very concretely how good it is.” If your problem satisfies that setup, then you can use AlphaEvolve, because unlike a human programmer who can try 10 things or 100 things or 1,000 things, AlphaEvolve can go on and on and on. It can come up with very counterintuitive strategies to solve that problem, some things that you might not have ever imagined.

items.question: How do you see human judgment helping to choose among equally effective mathematical solutions generated by AlphaEvolve?
items.object: Human judgment of AlphaEvolve’s mathematical solutions
items.answer: So we haven't used a human in the loop for AlphaEvolve, right? Most of our evaluators were programmatic evaluators. But imagine a hypothetical scenario where AlphaEvolve was told that you have to solve this math problem and come up with a new algorithm to solve this problem, and suppose it came up with many different kinds of solutions which are all equivalent in performance. Then which one is the best? The best is the one which is not only very effective on the problem, but is the most elegant according to a mathematician or the most simple to understand, right? And that's a very subjective human thing, like simplicity or interpretability. We don't have a crisp definition of it. It depends on—it is grounded in the human observer.

items.question: How do you decide whether a solution from AlphaEvolve needs validation in the physical world?
items.object: Real-world validation of AlphaEvolve's computationally evaluated solutions
items.answer: I think this goes back to how much do you trust the evaluator. If your evaluation was based on a computational method, and the computational method was perfect and you completely trusted it, then you don't have to. Then you think, “Well, I believe the computational model. The computational model says that the solution that AlphaEvolve came up with satisfies these properties. Job is done,” right? But if you don't believe that the computational model is the perfect characterization of reality, then you want to make sure that you validate that result in the real world, right? And you see whether that assessment of the evaluator was indeed correct.

items.question: How do you understand the significance of AlphaFold 2 for protein structure research?
items.object: AlphaFold 2's significance for protein structure research
items.answer: I'll give you the example of what happened with AlphaFold. We started working on this problem of protein structure prediction. For those of you who don't know, proteins are the building blocks of life. They are the Lego blocks of life. For many, many decades, scientists have been trying to figure out what the shape of proteins is, because if we understand the shape of proteins, we understand how they function, and we can use that to develop new drugs to treat the most challenging diseases on the planet. We can develop better enzymes and so on. Now, in 2021, as I mentioned, we released AlphaFold 2. Before that, it used to take one to five years, even for a single protein, to find the structure, and it might take a million dollars. There were some proteins so notoriously hard that people had been trying to study them for almost one or two decades and had not found the solution. Which is why only roughly 37% of human proteins had a known structure. After we released AlphaFold 2, because with AlphaFold 2 we could find the structure of all proteins, not just human proteins, all proteins on the planet, and we made the structures available to everyone on the planet, I went to a biology conference. After I gave my talk, a biologist approached me and said, “Push, I have been working on this protein for the last 10 years, and I had collected so much lab data to characterize this protein, to figure out its structure, but somehow this had eluded all kinds of investigation, and we still didn't know the structure.”

items.question: How do you understand AlphaFold 2’s impact on the work scientists can pursue in structural biology?
items.object: AlphaFold 2’s impact on structural biology
items.answer: I think it basically did three things. It first advanced structural biology. What was not possible earlier, which would take a synchrotron and six months and a million dollars, is now done in a second. Right? So it really advanced what was possible. Secondly, it accelerated it, and thirdly, it democratized it. That particular scientist working in Latin America or South Asia or Africa on some neglected tropical disease had no chance to figure out the structure of their protein. They did not have the funds or access to instruments that could find them the structure. Now they have access to those things, like any parasite that they're working on. So what do they do? They are now working in this new model where structures of proteins are not hard to get. They are everywhere. And so they are working on the next set of things, like how do you now use that knowledge to treat diseases and design better drugs?

They did not have the funds or access to instruments that could find them the structure. Now they have access to those things, like any parasite that they're working on. So what do they do? They are now working in this new model where structures of proteins are not hard to get. They are everywhere. And so they are working on the next set of things, like how do you now use that knowledge to treat diseases and design better drugs?

The response identifies AlphaFold 2 as making protein structures accessible to scientists who lack the resources for experimental structure determination.
The response explains that readily available protein structures shift scientists’ work from obtaining structures toward using structural knowledge to develop treatments.

items.question: How do you think AlphaEvolve will change the problems chip designers work on?
items.object: AlphaEvolve’s implications for chip design
items.answer: I think the same thing will happen with AlphaEvolve. You have these agents which can go beyond human abilities in solving these problems. Then the question becomes, which problems do we solve? What are the important characteristics of a chip that we need to improve on? We want to make it much more efficient, so that it requires less cooling, it requires less expensive construction mechanisms, it's more fault-tolerant. You can make the problem more and more sophisticated because now you have more sophisticated systems to optimize them.

items.question: How do you assess AlphaFold’s contribution to overcoming the bottlenecks in drug discovery?
items.object: AlphaFold's impact on drug discovery
items.answer: First, you have to understand a target. You have to understand: here's a protein in the body that I need to bind because this protein is somehow involved in the disease. So if I can somehow bind something to this protein and change its function, it will have an effect that can treat the disease. First you have to come up with that conjecture. Then you have to say, “Okay, now I have a target protein. How do I develop a drug? How do I develop a small molecule or another protein that binds to it?” So for that you needed to understand the structure of the protein, which other proteins it interacted with, and how it interacted with this molecule. This would take a significant amount of time, sometimes two years. Now that process is dramatically accelerated. Now you can do it in a few weeks or a month or a few months, what took you multiple years sometimes. But that's not the end of the story. After that you need to clinically validate it. So you have to go through phase one trials, phase two trials, phase three trials; you have to think about toxicity, all these other things. So what AlphaFold did was take one blocker away, make the overall timeline faster, but there are other blockers which our new generation of AI for biology models are hoping to accelerate and make much faster. So we have taken a big step, but we need to take a few more big steps.

But that's not the end of the story. After that you need to clinically validate it. So you have to go through phase one trials, phase two trials, phase three trials; you have to think about toxicity, all these other things.

So what AlphaFold did was take one blocker away, make the overall timeline faster, but there are other blockers which our new generation of AI for biology models are hoping to accelerate and make much faster. So we have taken a big step, but we need to take a few more big steps.

The response states that clinical validation remains a bottleneck in drug discovery despite AlphaFold’s advances.

items.question: How do you think about which domains will benefit most from AI?
items.object: The societal impact of AI across domains
items.answer: I think the question is, what domains do you think are important for society? Because AI is going to accelerate everything. It's going to accelerate healthcare, the ability for us to develop smarter systems, from healthcare to material science. If you think about the history of our civilization, we describe our civilization in the sense of there was first we were cave dwellers, and then we went into the Stone Age, and then we went to the Iron Age and the Bronze Age, and now, depending on who you talk to, you're either in the Silicon Age or in the Plastic Age, whether you're optimistic or feeling a bit sad. But if you take a step back and think about what humanity has achieved, what we have achieved compared to any other species is the ability to transform energy, to leverage energy. We have been able to leverage energy and do big things with that power. Now, if you can come up with, say, a new room-temperature superconductor that completely transforms your ability to handle energy, what changes will it bring about in society? They're hard to predict. If we can unlock fusion and energy becomes so cheap, if you think about geopolitics, if you think about the economy, a lot of it is about energy, and suddenly if energy goes down to zero, what will be the impact on the economics of the whole thing? Similarly, if you think about coding and you have these agents which can code, what does that mean? If everyone can code, intelligence is completely ubiquitous. Everyone has access to all these different things. So there will be dramatic changes, and everything will be impacted.

items.question: Where do you think we are in the emergence of AI-accelerated scientific discovery?
items.object: The era of AI-accelerated scientific discovery
items.answer: I think we are living through the middle of it. When you're in the middle, you don't really see it, but I think we are already in that era of AI-accelerated scientific discovery.

items.question: What do you see as the biggest bottlenecks to making AI-accelerated scientific discovery impactful?
items.object: Bottlenecks to AI-accelerated scientific discovery
items.answer: I think two elements. One is validation, bridging the gap between the digital and the real world, right? How do you validate some of that? So that is one key idea, and really capturing what is important for the problem. And the second bottleneck is how do you make this technology accessible? You can build the most sophisticated technology; if people don't know how to use it, then you will not have the impact that you want. AlphaFold 2 was not just impactful and transformative because it had very high accuracy, because even if it was quite accurate, it was not perfect. And suppose it was accurate on 99% of the things that it predicted—it's definitely not at 99%, probably at the 90 or 95% mark—but suppose it was accurate at 99%. The one person who got unlucky with their prediction and then spent the next one or two years chasing a wrong prediction would say that I should not use it, I should not use the predictions. So why is everyone using AlphaFold? They're using AlphaFold because not only is AlphaFold good at making predictions which are accurate, but it's also very good at understanding the limits of its predictions. When it makes mistakes, it basically holds its hand and says, “I have made a mistake.” So if it is making a prediction and saying, “I'm very confident,” most of the time it's correct, and that's great. This is something that the elements of today don't have. They don't have calibrated uncertainty.

items.question: What appeals to you about the wake-sleep algorithm?
items.object: The wake-sleep algorithm
items.answer: My favorite algorithm nobody talks about? Oh, the wake-sleep algorithm. Very few people know about it, but it's essentially the idea—it's a paper from MIT, from Kevin Ellis and Josh Tenenbaum, which talks about a way of doing training where you find some exploration and then somehow build the gist of it. Think about library construction. An analogy is library construction, right? You don't just want to write programs, but you also want to create the libraries that have common modules that will make all your future programs much easier to write.

items.question: How do you think about the relative importance of inference-time compute and training-time compute for improving AI models?
items.object: Inference-time compute and training-time compute
items.answer: I think inference-time compute will be very, very important. I think also test-time, sort of training-time compute will be equally important. We also—if you look at distillation, how powerful distillation has been, right? If these models have an ability to understand and conceptualize what these models are able to do and come up with better inherent representations, then they just become much more effective in making predictions. Maybe their uncertainty improves, and so on. They become more efficient even.

items.question: How do you assess the prospects for robotics?

items.answer: I'm bullish about everything. So I have to say bullish. I think everything will have an impact. But the question is basically near-term or longer-term, right? In the near term, getting robotics to work is challenging, but in the medium to long term I think I'm bullish.

items.question: How do you assess the advantage of the human form for humanoid robots?
items.object: Humanoid robots
items.answer: We have constructed our world for humans, right? We like the human form. A lot of the non-natural world around us is made for humans, has been designed for humans, from an architecture perspective. Humanoids have the same form as humans, so they will fit in all these different architectures that we have built. Now, whether they are the most optimal thing, that is not clear, but they certainly have an advantage that we designed everything for the human form, and now humanoids have the same form.

items.question: Do you think all future Nobel Prizes in the sciences will be won by teams working with AI?
items.object: AI's role in future Nobel Prize-winning scientific breakthroughs
items.answer: No, I think we are getting there, but humans are still winning Nobel Prizes in the sciences. I think there will come a point where AI will be indispensable, so it will be humans and AI teams working together to achieve these amazing breakthroughs.
